name: UDトーク (UD Talk)
oneLine: A Japanese app, on the market since 2013, that makes conversations visible: speech recognition and translation shared live to phones, browsers and projectors at lectures, events and offices, with word registration and corporate plans.

platforms.text: iPhone, iPad, Android, Kindle; PC app for editing
platforms.detail: Apps for iPhone and iPad, Android and Amazon Kindle. The Mac and Windows apps show and correct captions but have no speech recognition of their own. The Japanese App Store also lists Apple Watch, Apple silicon Macs and Apple Vision.

deviceRequirements.detail: The Japanese App Store lists iOS 15.0 or later for iPhone and iPad. The Android version needed is not stated on the pages we opened.

roomCaptions.detail: Tap the Tap to talk button, speak, and tap again to stop; the words appear as text. UD Talk says it is built mainly for people who speak into it on purpose, such as a lecturer, and points listeners who just hold a phone to the iPhone's built-in Live Captions.

groupConversations.text: Captions shared to phones, browsers and projectors
groupConversations.detail: A talk can be published with a QR code: other phones join to speak, only to read, or to correct mistakes. Publishing on the web shows it in any browser without the app, and a projector or full-screen view puts it on a big screen. Each person can also speak into their own phone.

speakerLabels.text: Name set on each phone; file tool labels up to 10
speakerLabels.detail: When each person speaks into their own phone, their lines carry the name set in that phone's UD Talk. Telling voices apart on one phone is not described; the developer suggests people say their name before they speak. The separate Subtitle Editor for files can label up to 10 speakers.

voiceNames.detail: A 2018 post said voice identification was not adopted. A later note on the same post says identification that needs advance registration has been added, without describing how it works.

speakerDirection.detail: UD Talk's pages don't describe showing which direction a voice comes from.

translation.text: Yes, live, with a re-translation check
translation.detail: Speech can be recognised in many languages and translated live. Re-translation back into your own language lets you check the result before relying on it. The free app uses Google Translate.

languages.detail: Japanese uses the AmiVoice engine. In the free version, other languages use the phone's own speech recognition (Apple on iOS, Google on Android); paid plans use Google Cloud on both. A list of recognition and translation language settings published in December 2020 has 173 language and region entries; no newer count is published.

offline.text: iPhone only, with the Apple On Device engine
offline.detail: On iOS, switching to the Apple On Device engine captions without internet. Its FAQ says recognition and translation otherwise run on servers and need a connection.

saveTranscripts.text: Yes, logs; audio too on iPhone
saveTranscripts.detail: Conversation logs stay in the app and older ones can be found by date. On iPhone, the audio can be saved with the talk and played back next to the text.

export.text: Email or share logs, as text with times
export.detail: Logs are sent by email or shared from the menu, as a list of text with timing information. A separate web tool turns them into subtitles.

fileUpload.text: Separate web tool, pay per use
fileUpload.detail: The app captions live speech. Subtitle Editor for Files, a separate web tool, transcribes audio and video files, priced per use; corporate plans include 10 hours a month of Subtitle Editor Lite.

summaries.detail: A beta web tool summarises a UD Talk log (.csv) or a subtitle file (.srt), using ChatGPT. It is not part of the app.

customWords.text: Yes, word registration and shared dictionaries
customWords.detail: Words can be registered in the app or on a website, and public dictionaries can be switched per conversation. Registered words only work with the AmiVoice engine.

display.text: UD fonts, colours, text size; kanji in hiragana
display.detail: Readable UD fonts can be chosen, and the web view sets background colour, text size and whether speaker names show. Kanji a child has not learned yet can be shown in hiragana by school grade.

soundAlerts.detail: UD Talk's pages don't describe alerts for sounds such as a doorbell or an alarm.

phoneCalls.detail: Its pages describe conversations, events and online meetings, not phone calls.

videoCalls.detail: One device set up with Zoom's caption token sends the captions into the meeting, with the name of the phone that spoke. A phone next to the computer can also caption the meeting audio.

mediaOnDevice.detail: Captioning videos or audio playing on the same phone is not described.

humanCaptioners.text: People correct live; partners staff events
humanCaptioners.detail: Other phones and the Mac or Windows app can correct mistakes while captions run. For events, partner companies run UD Talk with editors and re-speakers, quoted individually.

signLanguage.detail: Theater Mode lays the captions over the camera picture, so the speaker or a sign language interpreter and the captions can be watched together. No sign language translation is described.

privacy.text: Cloud; the free version reuses speech data
privacy.detail: Speech is sent to servers for recognition. In the free version, your voice and the text made from it are collected and reused to improve recognition; the Compact Plan, corporate plans and the App Introduction Program discard voice data. On iPhone, the Apple On Device engine keeps recognition on the phone.

account.text: No account for the free app
account.detail: Install, agree to the licence and tap Tap to talk. Corporate plans come with an account, and a free account for registering words on the web is optional.

availability.text: Japan; also in the US and other App Stores
availability.detail: Made in Japan, with the app in Japanese and English. The App Store lookup also returns it in the US store (November 2026), and it is on Google Play.

freePlan.text: Free, also for business; not for schools or city halls
freePlan.detail: Individuals and companies can use the free version, also commercially. Government offices, local authorities, schools and public facilities may not use it for their work, except for disaster prevention and evacuation shelters. Its voice data is reused, and support is the online manual only.

price.detail: In-app Compact Plan on the Japanese App Store, November 2026; Google Play lists the same. Corporate plans, per year before tax: ¥117,600 (small organisations), ¥216,000 (schools), ¥324,000 (standard, one site) or ¥888,000 (premium, no site limit), plus a setup fee.

accessibilityFunding.text: Free accounts for public bodies and interpreters
accessibilityFunding.detail: Not a government programme. Shamrock Records lends a free corporate account to government offices, local authorities, schools and public facilities that agree to be listed as users, and to sign language interpreters and summary writers registered with a local authority's dispatch service.

strengths.text: Captions can be shared live to other phones by QR code, to any browser without the app, to a projector and into Zoom.
Words can be registered in the app or on the web, and other people can correct mistakes live from their own devices.
The free version may be used commercially, and the Compact Plan costs ¥500 a month on the Japanese App Store (November 2026).
Paid plans discard voice data, and public bodies and registered interpreters can get a corporate account for free.

limits.text: In the free version, your voice and the text made from it are collected and reused to improve recognition.
Government offices, local authorities and schools may not use the free version for their work.
Offline recognition is iPhone only, and saving audio with the text is iOS only.
File transcription and summaries are separate web tools, not part of the app.

notes: Conflicts: (1) Price: the Japanese App Store description still says the Compact Plan is 980 yen a month or 480 yen a week with a 3-day trial, but the same listing's In-App Purchases list shows ¥500 (1 month) and ¥300 (1 week), Google Play's description says 500 and 300 yen, and the Compact Plan page says the price fell to ¥500 and ¥300 (its heading says from 6 February 2022, its price lines say from 6 February 2025). The plan comparison table on udtalk.jp/compare2/ is an image from August 2024 that still shows ¥980/¥480. The table uses the In-App Purchases list. (2) Offline: the FAQ says recognition and translation need internet; the 'five things' post says the iOS app can use Apple's offline engine. Both are reflected. (3) Speaker identification: the 2018 post says voiceprint identification was not adopted; an undated note added to it (last updated 2 February 2022) says identification needing advance registration is now implemented, without details; the Subtitle Editor for files labels up to 10 speakers. Marked not_stated for remembering voices. (4) Apple Watch: the Japanese App Store lists Apple Watch (watchOS 9.0) as compatible; a 2015 post announced a Watch version.
